"A lot of these kids don't know how to work out, or that they even have the capacity to work out. # Atlanta Non-Profit Tackles Childhood Obesity One Boot Camp at a Time

**ATLANTA (CNN)** — On a crisp Saturday morning in a park just outside downtown Atlanta, a group of teenagers jogs, jumps, and pushes through a series of exercises that would challenge many adults. They're participants in the FitWit Foundation's six-week fitness boot camp, a program designed to combat a growing health crisis affecting millions of young Americans.

The FitWit Foundation, a local non-profit, has spent years working to change the trajectory of teen health in Atlanta's underserved communities, offering free fitness instruction, nutrition education, and mentorship to adolescents who might otherwise lack access to such resources.

## A Growing Crisis

The stakes could hardly be higher. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, childhood obesity affects approximately 1 in 5 children and adolescents in the United States. The CDC reports that obesity prevalence was nearly 20% among children and teens ages 2 to 19, a figure that has more than tripled since the 1970s.

The health consequences are significant. The CDC notes that children with obesity are at higher risk for developing serious conditions such as type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and cardiovascular disease—problems once seen almost exclusively in adults.

## More Than Just Exercise

For the instructors at FitWit, the mission goes beyond physical fitness.

"We're not just here to make these kids do push-ups," said Marcus Reynolds, a lead instructor with the program. "We're here to change how they think about their bodies, their health, and what they're capable of. When a teenager realizes they can run a mile when they couldn't before, that confidence spills over into every part of their life."

Reynolds, who has worked with the foundation for several years, emphasized that the program meets participants where they are.

"A lot of these kids have never been taught how to move, how to eat, how to take care of themselves," he said. "We start with the basics, and we celebrate every small victory. By week six, the transformation—not just physically, but mentally—is incredible to watch."

## A Success Story

Few embody that transformation better than 15-year-old Jasmine Carter, who joined the boot camp last spring at her mother's urging.

"When I started, I couldn't even finish the warm-up without stopping," Jasmine recalled. "I hated it. I wanted to quit after the first day."

But she didn't. Over the next six weeks, Jasmine gradually built her endurance, learned to prepare healthier meals, and formed friendships with other participants facing similar struggles. By the end of the program, she had lost weight, but more importantly, she said, she had gained something else.

"I feel like a different person," Jasmine said, smiling. "I have energy now. I joined my school's track team, which I never thought I'd do in a million years. FitWit didn't just change my body—it changed my whole life."

Her mother, Denise Carter, said the difference has been remarkable.

"I got my daughter back," she said. "She's happier, she's more confident, and she's making healthier choices on her own now. I can't thank this program enough."

## Looking Ahead

The FitWit Foundation hopes to expand its reach in the coming years, bringing its model to more neighborhoods across metro Atlanta. With childhood obesity rates remaining stubbornly high nationwide, organizers say the need has never been greater.

"Every kid deserves a chance to be healthy," Reynolds said. "We're just trying to give them the tools and the belief that they can do it. The rest is up to them—and they always surprise us."

For families interested in learning more or enrolling their teens, the foundation offers information through its community outreach programs and local partnerships.

*As childhood obesity continues to challenge communities across the country, grassroots efforts like the FitWit Foundation offer a reminder that meaningful change often begins one step—and one push-up—at a time.*

# Sweating for the Season: How One After-School Boot Camp Is Giving Teens the Gift of Health

*A local charity program transforms lives one push-up at a time, proving the best holiday gifts don't come wrapped in paper.*

---

On a chilly December evening, while most of the neighborhood settles in for hot cocoa and holiday movies, the gymnasium at Lincoln Community Center is buzzing with an entirely different kind of energy. Music thumps through the speakers. Sneakers squeak across the polished floor. And a group of teenagers—laughing, groaning, and cheering each other on—are discovering something powerful: they're stronger than they ever imagined.

Welcome to **Team Transformation**, a free after-school boot camp that's become the season's most unexpected gift for dozens of local families.

## A Program Born From Compassion

Modeled loosely on the hit television series *The Biggest Loser*, the program swaps reality-show drama for genuine community support. There are no eliminations here, no contestants sent home. Instead, teens work in teams, celebrate collective milestones, and learn that fitness is a journey best traveled together.

"We took the parts that inspired people—the transformations, the teamwork, the 'you can do this' spirit—and left behind anything that felt like shame or competition," explains program founder Maria Delgado, a former physical education teacher who launched Team Transformation three years ago. "These kids don't need another place to feel judged. They need a place to feel capable."

The results speak for themselves. Since opening its doors, the program has served more than 200 teenagers, offering free access to certified trainers, nutritional guidance, and—perhaps most importantly—a sense of belonging.

## More Than Just Weight Loss

Sixteen-year-old Marcus Bell joined the program last spring after struggling with his confidence and energy levels. Today, he arrives early to help set up equipment and welcome newcomers.

"I used to dread gym class. I felt like everyone was watching me," Marcus says, wiping sweat from his forehead after leading his team through a round of squats. "Here, nobody's laughing. Everyone's just trying to get better. Now I actually *want* to move. I feel like myself again."

That transformation—the shift from self-doubt to self-belief—is exactly what Delgado hoped to inspire. While participants have collectively lost hundreds of pounds, she's quick to emphasize that the scale tells only part of the story.

"We measure success in smiles, in kids who start speaking up in class, in parents who tell us their teenager is sleeping better and stressing less," she says. "Health isn't just a number. It's how you feel when you wake up in the morning."

## The Gift of Giving Back

As the holidays approach, Team Transformation has taken on a spirit of generosity that extends beyond the gym walls. This month, participants are organizing a community wellness fair, where they'll share healthy recipes, lead beginner-friendly workouts, and mentor younger children interested in joining next year.

"These teens came to us for help, and now they're the ones giving back," Delgado beams. "That's the real gift of the season."

The program runs entirely on donations and volunteer hours. Local businesses have chipped in with equipment, gym space, and healthy snacks. A nearby grocery store donates fresh produce weekly. And a team of volunteer trainers gives up their evenings to coach the next generation toward healthier lives.

"This is my favorite thing I do all year," says volunteer trainer Devon Price, who works as a firefighter by day. "You watch these kids walk in nervous and unsure, and you watch them walk out standing a little taller. There's no better feeling, especially this time of year."

## A Season of New Beginnings

For fifteen-year-old Aliyah Johnson, the program has become a second family.

"My mom works two jobs, so afternoons used to be lonely," she admits. "Now I have people who check on me, who cheer for me. Last week I did a full plank for the first time, and the whole team started clapping. I almost cried."

As the evening session winds down, the teens gather in a circle for their closing tradition: each person shares one thing they're grateful for. Tonight, the answers range from "my legs don't hurt as much anymore" to "these guys, my friends."

Outside, snow begins to fall softly on the parking lot. Inside, a group of young people—breathing hard, hearts full—are proving that the greatest gifts aren't found under a tree.

They're found in the courage to change, the kindness of a community, and the simple, radical belief that every teenager deserves the chance to feel healthy, strong, and seen.

---

---

# Fighting Fit: How One Atlanta Program Takes On Childhood Obesity

*A community-based initiative offers a model for reversing troubling national trends*

---

ATLANTA — On a warm Saturday morning in southwest Atlanta, a group of a dozen children race across a community center gymnasium, laughing as they dribble basketballs and dodge cones. For the participants in this program, the scene represents more than recreation—it's part of a comprehensive effort to combat one of the most persistent public health challenges facing American children.

## A Growing Crisis

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, childhood obesity affects approximately 14.7 million children and adolescents in the United States. The most recent CDC data indicates that obesity prevalence among children and teens ages 2 to 19 stands at roughly 19.7 percent—a figure that has more than tripled since the 1970s.

The disparities are striking. CDC statistics show that obesity rates are higher among Hispanic children (26.2 percent) and non-Hispanic Black children (24.8 percent) compared to non-Hispanic white children (16.6 percent). Socioeconomic factors compound the problem, with children from lower-income households facing elevated risks.

Georgia has historically ranked among states with higher childhood obesity rates, making local intervention efforts particularly urgent.

## A Community-Based Response

*Note: The following organization is presented as a representative example of the community-based programs operating in this space.*

Programs like those modeled on Atlanta's community health initiatives typically combine physical activity, nutrition education, and family engagement to address obesity from multiple angles.

"You can't solve this problem by simply telling kids to exercise more," said a pediatric health specialist familiar with such interventions. "These children often live in food deserts, lack safe spaces to play, and face barriers their families can't easily overcome. Effective programs address the whole environment."

The most successful models share several characteristics:

- **After-school fitness programming** that makes physical activity fun and social
- **Nutrition workshops** for both children and parents
- **Access to fresh produce** through partnerships with local farmers markets or community gardens
- **Health screenings** to track progress and identify medical concerns

## Voices from the Ground

For families enrolled in these programs, the impact can be transformative.

A parent whose child participated in a similar Atlanta-area initiative described noticeable changes: "My daughter used to spend all her time on the couch. Now she asks to go outside. She's learning about vegetables and actually wants to help cook dinner. That's something I never expected."

Program staff emphasize that psychological changes often matter as much as physical ones.

"We see kids gain confidence," noted one program coordinator. "When a child who thought they could never run a mile finally does it, something shifts. That self-belief carries into everything else."

## What the Experts Say

Public health researchers stress that community programs, while valuable, work best as part of broader systemic change.

"Individual programs can change individual lives, and that matters enormously," said a professor of public health specializing in nutrition policy. "But to move the needle on national obesity rates, we also need policy changes—better school lunches, improved access to healthy food, urban planning that encourages activity, and reduced marketing of unhealthy foods to children."

The CDC has endorsed a multi-sector approach, recommending investments in early childhood settings, schools, and communities simultaneously.

## Measuring Success

Evaluating obesity programs presents challenges. Experts caution against focusing solely on weight, which can stigmatize children and overlook important gains in fitness, dietary habits, and mental health.

"We measure success in multiple ways," the program coordinator explained. "Are kids moving more? Are they eating better? Do they feel good about themselves? Weight is just one piece."

Research on community-based interventions has shown mixed but promising results, with the most effective programs demonstrating sustained engagement and family involvement as key predictors of success.

## Looking Ahead

As childhood obesity remains a national concern, advocates argue that scalable, community-rooted programs offer one of the most promising paths forward—particularly in underserved communities where the need is greatest.

Back in the gymnasium, as the basketball game winds down and children line up for water and fruit, the immediate benefits are clear on their faces. Whether such programs can help reverse a decades-long national trend remains an open question—but for the families involved, the answer already feels personal.

*By CNN Health Staff*

As childhood obesity rates climb and screen time replaces playtime, health experts are sounding the alarm about a growing crisis: American teenagers are increasingly abandoning physical activity, with potentially lasting consequences for their health.

According to recent health data, a significant portion of teens fail to meet the recommended 60 minutes of daily physical activity. The reasons are familiar to any parent—smartphones, streaming services, reduced physical education budgets, and busy schedules that leave little room for exercise.

"We're seeing a generation that's more sedentary than any before it," said Dr. Marcus Reynolds, a pediatric health specialist not affiliated with the program. "The habits kids form now will follow them into adulthood."

## An Unconventional Approach

One nonprofit organization is fighting back with a strategy that meets teens where they are: their love of technology. **FitForward**, a community-based program operating in several school districts, offers participants tangible rewards—including popular gadgets like the iPod Nano—for hitting personalized fitness milestones.

"We know that telling a 15-year-old that exercise is 'good for them' isn't exactly a winning pitch," said Angela Torres, FitForward's program director. "But give them a goal, a little friendly competition, and a reward they actually want? Suddenly they're showing up early to log their workouts."

The program tracks activity through wearable pedometers and check-ins, awarding points that students can redeem for prizes. Bigger goals—like consistent participation over several months—unlock the coveted electronics.

## Kids Are Responding

For many participants, the incentive was just the nudge they needed.

"Honestly, I signed up for the iPod," admitted Jayden Michaels, 14, laughing. "But now I actually like running with my friends. We push each other. I feel better, and I'm sleeping better too."

Sixteen-year-old Sophia Nguyen said the program changed her relationship with fitness entirely. "I used to think I just wasn't an athletic person. Turns out I just needed a reason to start. Earning something made it feel real."

## Beyond the Prizes

Staff emphasize that the rewards are only the entry point. The real goal is building lasting habits.

"The gadget gets them in the door," Torres said. "But what keeps them is the community, the confidence, and honestly just feeling good. We've had kids keep exercising long after they earned their prize. That's the win."

Still, some critics question whether external rewards can create genuine, self-sustaining motivation.

"There's always a debate about intrinsic versus extrinsic motivation," Dr. Reynolds noted. "But if a reward system gets a kid off the couch and helps them discover they enjoy being active, I'd call that a success. The key is transitioning them to internal motivation over time."

## A Growing Need

With physical education programs facing budget cuts nationwide, community organizations like FitForward are increasingly filling the gap.

"Schools can't do it alone anymore," Torres said. "It takes families, communities, and yes, sometimes a little creativity—and a good prize—to get kids moving again."

For teens like Jayden, the results speak for themselves.

"My mom keeps saying she can't believe I ask to go running now," he said. "Neither can I."

# FitWit Boot Camp Transforms Teen Fitness, One Six-Week Session at a Time

**Local program combines exercise, nutrition, and mentorship to deliver measurable results for area youth**

When 15-year-old Marcus Chen first walked into the FitWit fitness boot camp six weeks ago, he could barely complete a single lap around the track. Last Saturday, he crossed the finish line of the program's final fitness challenge having run a full mile—and beaming with pride.

"I didn't think I could do it," Marcus said, catching his breath. "But the coaches never let me quit, and neither did the other kids. We pushed each other."

Marcus is one of dozens of teenagers who have completed FitWit, a growing boot camp program designed specifically for participants ages 13 to 18. The program has earned attention for its structured approach and, more importantly, its documented outcomes.

## How the Program Works

FitWit operates on a six-week cycle, with participants meeting three times per week for 75-minute sessions. Each session blends cardiovascular training, strength-building exercises, and flexibility work, all scaled to accommodate teens of varying fitness levels.

"We're not trying to turn every kid into an athlete," said program director Tanya Roberts, a certified fitness instructor who founded FitWit four years ago. "We're teaching them that movement can be fun, that their bodies are capable of more than they think, and that healthy habits are for life."

The program is divided into three components:

- **Physical conditioning:** Circuit training, team-based challenges, and progressive workouts that increase in intensity each week.
- **Nutrition education:** Weekly workshops where teens learn to read food labels, plan balanced meals, and understand how food fuels performance.
- **Mentorship and goal-setting:** Each participant is paired with a coach who tracks progress and helps set personalized benchmarks.

## Measurable Results

What sets FitWit apart, according to Roberts, is its emphasis on tracking real data. At the start and end of each session, participants complete baseline assessments measuring endurance, strength, and flexibility.

According to the program's most recent internal report, the current cohort of 28 teens saw:

- An average **22 percent improvement** in cardiovascular endurance, measured by timed running and step tests.
- A **35 percent increase** in the number of push-ups and sit-ups participants could complete in one minute.
- Improved flexibility scores across roughly 80 percent of participants.

Beyond the physical metrics, Roberts pointed to gains that are harder to quantify but equally important. "We see confidence go up. We see kids making friends. Parents tell us their teenagers are sleeping better and feeling more focused at school."

## Personal Stories

For 16-year-old Aisha Williams, FitWit was about more than fitness numbers.

"I was really shy, and I didn't have a lot of friends," Aisha said. "The team stuff made me talk to people I never would have talked to. Now we hang out outside of camp. I feel like a totally different person."

Her mother, Denise Williams, said the change has been remarkable. "She used to spend all weekend on her phone. Now she's asking me to take her on runs. It's like she found a part of herself she didn't know was there."

For others, the impact has been physical and emotional at once. Fourteen-year-old Jordan Bailey joined the program after struggling with self-confidence.

"I used to hate gym class because I felt like everybody was better than me," Jordan said. "Here, nobody made fun of you. Everyone was just trying to get better. I actually look forward to coming now."

## Looking Ahead

Buoyed by strong results and word-of-mouth referrals, FitWit plans to expand to a second location next year and add a summer intensive program. Roberts said scholarships are available to ensure cost is not a barrier for interested families.

"Every teenager deserves the chance to feel strong and capable," Roberts said. "That's what we're here to give them—six weeks at a time."

Registration for the next FitWit session opens next month. Families interested in learning more can visit the program's website or attend an upcoming open house.

*Editor's note: Participant results cited in this story are based on figures provided by the FitWit program.*
